items.prose:
**Verdict:** Not confirmed: momentum ran in the predicted direction with a positive long/short Sharpe, but the result does not clear the statistical bar for confirmation given the short sample.

**Hypothesis:** 12-month momentum (mom_12_1, 12-month return skipping the most recent month) predicts that high-momentum stocks outperform low-momentum stocks cross-sectionally.

**Method:** Point-in-time S&P 500 universe, 2022-10-31 to 2026-10-01 (983 invested days), decile sort, dollar-neutral long/short, monthly rebalance, 10bps one-way cost, 1 trial run.

**Results:**

| Variant | Sharpe | CAGR | Max DD | P(beats best of N) | Clears 0.95 gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mom 12-1, decile L/S, 10bps | 0.35 | 5.9% | -32.8% | 0.751 | No |

**Robustness:**
- Bucket shape: a fairly good staircase (Spearman 0.72), though the lowest-momentum bucket (bucket 1) still returned 12.3% annualised versus 23.0% for the top bucket, so the bottom leg is noisy rather than cleanly losing.
- Two halves: Sharpe was 0.07 in the first half of the sample and 0.55 in the second half, so the effect was concentrated in the more recent period.
- Costs: Sharpe was 0.40 at zero cost and 0.27 at 25bps, so the effect survives trading costs but shrinks.

**What would change this:** A longer history (the tool itself flags a minimum track record length of 5765 days, far beyond the 983 observed) would let the deflated Sharpe be judged properly; consistent out-of-sample strength across both halves and additional independent samples would be needed before concluding the effect is real rather than a short-sample artifact.

items.hypothesis: Do low-volatility stocks outperform high-volatility stocks?
items.prose:
**Verdict:** Contradicted: low-volatility stocks did not outperform high-volatility stocks over this sample, the long/short spread ran strongly in the opposite direction with low probability of being a genuine effect.

**Hypothesis:** Stocks with lower realised volatility (21-day or 63-day annualised) outperform stocks with higher realised volatility, tested as a long low-vol / short high-vol decile spread.

**Method:** Point-in-time S&P 500 universe, 2021-11-30 to 2026-10-01 (vol_21d) and 2022-01-31 to 2026-10-01 (vol_63d), 10 buckets, dollar-neutral long/short, monthly rebalance, 10 bps one-way cost, 2 trials run.

**Results:**

| Variant | Sharpe | CAGR | Max DD | P(beats best of N) | Clears 0.95 gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| vol_21d (low minus high) | -0.59 | -16.9% | -67.0% | 0.032 | No |
| vol_63d (low minus high) | -0.65 | -20.1% | -70.8% | 0.026 | No |

**Robustness:**
- Bucket returns are strongly monotonic but inverted relative to the hypothesis (Spearman 0.93 and 0.92): the lowest-volatility decile returned 3.5% to 4.7% annualised while the highest-volatility decile returned 15.9% to 21.6%, i.e. volatility paid off rather than hurting.
- Both halves of the sample are negative for the low-vol spread, and the effect worsens sharply in the second half (sharpe_second_half -1.08 and -1.22 vs -0.09 and -0.07 in the first half), so this is not a one-period artifact.
- The result holds at every cost level tested (0, 10, 25 bps), so it is not a transaction-cost illusion; the sign is robustly negative throughout.

**What would change this:** A longer sample spanning a full market cycle including a sharp drawdown (low-vol effects typically show up in down markets, and this window may have been dominated by a strong, volatility-rewarding rally), or repeating the test on the full S&P 500 point-in-time universe over a decade instead of five years.

items.hypothesis: Do low-volatility stocks outperform, on point-in-time membership?
items.prose:
## Findings: Low-volatility effect on point-in-time S&P 500 membership

**Setup:** Fetched the point-in-time universe (549 tickers, 2012-12-27 through 2026-09-03 snapshots, 268,050 rows). Computed three volatility-family features and ran dollar-neutral long/short decile spreads (10 buckets, monthly rebalance, 10 bps cost) — the correct test for this cross-sectional hypothesis, since long-only results would embed market beta that can't be isolated here.

| Feature | Sharpe (annualised) | n_invested_days | prob_sharpe_above_zero | prob_beats_best_of_n_trials (deflated) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vol_21d (21d realized vol) | 1.057964 | 460 | 0.9226 | 0.8097 |
| vol_63d (63d realized vol) | 1.342857 | 419 | 0.9572 | 0.8847 |
| ivol_63d (63d idiosyncratic vol vs SPY) | 1.252554 | 419 | 0.9446 | 0.8594 |

All three backtests go long low-vol / short high-vol (that's what the tool's bucket sort with long_short=True does for a low-vol hypothesis — low decile long, high decile short), and all three post positive, superficially attractive Sharpe ratios in the 1.06–1.34 range.

**But the deflated numbers say otherwise.** `prob_beats_best_of_n_trials` — the actual deflated-Sharpe metric, accounting for the 3 trials run in this session — comes in at 0.8097, 0.8847, and 0.8594. These are probabilities that the strategy's true Sharpe beats the best of 3 worthless comparison strategies, not confidence in the effect itself. The eval gate for confirming an effect is 0.95; none of the three clears it, though they are above the 0.5 "coin-flip" line, which the tool documentation explicitly says is *not* support.

Additionally, `min_track_record_length_days` — the sample length needed before the Sharpe could be statistically distinguished from zero given its volatility — is 614.3 days for vol_21d, 383.9 days for vol_63d, and 445.6 days for ivol_63d. The actual invested samples are only 460, 419, and 419 days respectively. Two of the three (vol_21d, ivol_63d... actually check: vol_63d's required 383.9 < observed 419, ivol's required 445.6 > observed 419, vol_21d's required 614.3 > observed 460) fall short of or barely clear the minimum track record needed, meaning the sample is too short relative to the volatility of the strategy's returns to have real confidence in the sign of the true Sharpe.

**Conclusion:** The evidence is suggestive but not sufficient to confirm the low-volatility effect on this point-in-time sample. All three vol-based long/short spreads show positive raw Sharpe ratios, but once deflated for the 3 trials tried, none reaches the 0.95 confirmation bar (best is 0.8847 for vol_63d), and the track record (~419–460 invested days) is close to or shorter than the minimum length needed to statistically distinguish the Sharpe from zero for two of the three variants. This looks like a promising but statistically unconfirmed signal over a fairly short (roughly 1.7-year) invested window — not a validated outperformance claim. A longer sample and/or fewer exploratory trials would be needed to make this conclusive.

items.hypothesis: Do stocks that went up over the last year keep going up, on point-in-time membership?
items.prose:
## Findings: 12‑1 Momentum, Point‑in‑Time S&P 500 Membership

**Setup:** Point‑in-time panel (549 tickers, 268,186 rows, snapshots from 2012‑12‑27, though the momentum feature only had 252-day history built up starting 2025‑09‑08, giving 238 invested days / ~1 year of live backtest). Decile sort on `mom_12_1`, monthly rebalance, 10 bps cost.

### Long/short (top decile winners minus bottom decile losers) — the actual test of the hypothesis
- Sharpe: **0.454389** (annualised)
- CAGR: 10.6403%, annualised vol 39.2758%, max drawdown ‑33.4396%
- `prob_sharpe_above_zero`: **0.6693**
- `prob_beats_best_of_n_trials` (deflated Sharpe, n_trials=2): **0.579**
- `min_track_record_length_days`: **3342.0** days (≈13.3 years) needed to distinguish this Sharpe from zero — far more than the 238 days actually observed.

### Long-only tilt (top decile only) — NOT a test of the cross-sectional hypothesis
- Sharpe: 1.295908, CAGR 40.2577%, max drawdown ‑19.9331%
- `prob_beats_best_of_n_trials`: 0.844
- This number is contaminated by market beta (holding a concentrated long book in a rising-market year) and cannot be used to support or refute the momentum hypothesis — there's no benchmark subtraction available here to isolate skill from beta.

### Conclusion
The dollar-neutral long/short spread — the correct test of "do past winners keep winning" — produced a positive but weak Sharpe (0.454389), with only a 66.93% probability of being genuinely above zero, and a deflated-Sharpe probability of 0.579 (barely above the 0.5 coin-flip threshold with just 2 trials run). The minimum track record length required to trust this Sharpe is about 3,342 days (~13.3 years), but the backtest only covers 238 invested days. 

**The evidence does not support the hypothesis with any confidence.** The long-only result looks much stronger (Sharpe 1.295908) but that reflects the tilted book's exposure to what appears to have been a strong market/momentum-cohort year overall, not a validated cross-sectional momentum effect — it should not be quoted as confirmation. A much longer sample (multiple years, ideally a full decade-plus given the point-in-time membership data goes back to 2012) would be needed before this Sharpe could be distinguished from noise.

These are my final two backtests, so I'll report these `analyze_results` figures directly (n_trials_used=2, matching the two backtests actually run).

## Findings: 12-1 Momentum on Point-in-Time S&P 500 Membership

**The hypothesis test (long/short, dollar-neutral decile spread)** is the correct isolation of the cross-sectional momentum effect:

- Sharpe (annualised): **0.454389**
- Total return over window: **0.100205** (CAGR 0.106403), ann. vol 0.392758, max drawdown -0.334396
- n_invested_days: 238 (roughly the first year is unscored, since mom_12_1 needs 252 days of history — first_date_with_values was 2025-09-08)
- **prob_sharpe_above_zero: 0.6693**
- **prob_beats_best_of_n_trials: 0.579** (this is the deflated-Sharpe result)
- **min_track_record_length_days: 3342.0** — i.e., you'd need about 3342 trading days (~13 years) of this kind of return stream to be confident the true Sharpe is distinguishable from zero
- n_trials_used: 2

**Interpretation:** A prob_beats_best_of_n_trials of 0.579 is only marginally above the 0.5 coin-flip line, and the required track record (3342 days) is more than 10x longer than what we actually have (238 invested days). The long/short spread is positive but the evidence is weak — this is exactly the "high Sharpe on a short sample" situation that should not be oversold.

**The long-only decile 10 result** (Sharpe 1.295908, prob_beats_best_of_n_trials 0.844) looks much stronger, but per the tool's own caveat, long-only portfolios carry market beta that no tool here can separate out. Given that the invested window was a strong bull period for momentum names generally, this Sharpe most likely reflects broad market/momentum-tilted beta exposure during 2025, not evidence for the cross-sectional hypothesis. It is not a valid test of "do winners keep winning relative to losers" — for that, only the long/short number counts.

**Bottom line:** On point-in-time membership, over the available ~238-day invested window, cross-sectional 12-1 momentum shows a positive but statistically weak long/short spread (Sharpe 0.454389, deflated-probability 0.579, needing ~3342 days of track record to be confident it's non-zero — we have 238). This is not strong enough evidence to confirm the momentum-continuation hypothesis; it's consistent with either a real but modest effect or noise. The long-only number, while eye-catching, cannot be used to support the hypothesis because it conflates market beta with the momentum tilt. A longer sample (multiple years of scored history, not just one year of overlap after the 252-day burn-in) would be needed to draw a confident conclusion.

items.hypothesis: do stocks that went up over the last year keep going up?
items.prose:
These are my final backtests (n_trials_used=2 matches the actual count), so these numbers are the ones to report.

## Findings: Does 12-month momentum (skipping the last month) persist?

**Setup:** 549-ticker universe, mom_12_1 feature (12-month return skipping most recent month), decile sort, monthly rebalance, 10bps costs. The feature requires 252 days of history, so despite ~2 years of raw data, the *invested* window is only 238 trading days (~1 year, Sept 2025–present).

**The correct test — long/short decile spread (isolates the cross-sectional effect):**
- Sharpe: 0.65 (annualised)
- Max drawdown: -32%
- prob_sharpe_above_zero: 0.73
- **prob_beats_best_of_n_trials (deflated Sharpe signal): 0.65** — above 0.5, but not decisively so
- Minimum track record length needed: **1,655 days** (~6.6 years) to statistically distinguish this Sharpe from zero

**Long-only (top decile), for reference only — NOT a test of the hypothesis:**
- Sharpe: 1.48, prob_beats_best_of_n: 0.88
- This number includes market beta with no way to strip it out here. The window (Sept 2025 onward) may simply have been a strong up-market, in which case a long-only momentum tilt looks great regardless of any cross-sectional momentum effect. It should not be cited as evidence for "momentum persists."

### Bottom line
The hypothesis is meant to be tested by the long/short spread, and that spread gives a modest positive Sharpe (0.65) with a 65% probability of beating the best of the two strategies tried — better than a coin flip, but well short of a confident result. Critically, **the minimum track record length is ~1,655 trading days (~6.6 years), and we only have 238 days of invested data** — roughly a 7x shortfall. This means the data we have is nowhere near enough to say with statistical confidence that this Sharpe ratio is distinguishable from zero, even though the point estimate is positive.

**Honest conclusion:** The evidence is suggestive but insufficient. There's a positive momentum spread in this sample, but the track record is far too short to confirm it's real skill/effect rather than noise. The long-only Sharpe of 1.48 looks impressive but reflects market exposure over a single one-year window and says nothing reliable about whether "stocks that went up keep going up" in a market-neutral sense. To make this convincing, we'd need several more years of invested history (ideally >1,600 trading days) and/or corroborating evidence across different regimes and universes.
